catalog_quote: Kham is interpreted as having no function for stress. Watters (2002: 23-4) reports that in bisyllabic and polysyllabic words with monomoraic syllables there is "no discernable stress" but that in trisyllabic forms "there is discernable stress on the final syllable". Elsewhere stress is perceived on final long syllables. These perceptions of stress may be illusory.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand only: per Watters 2002 (as summarised by LAPSyD), Takale Kham has no functional word stress; words made of light (monomoraic) syllables show no discernible stress, while trisyllabic words and words ending in a long syllable are perceived with stress on the final syllable. Tone (pitch pattern + voice register) is the contrastive prosody of the word.
new_statements.exceptions: As reported: no discernible stress in bisyllabic/polysyllabic words whose syllables are all monomoraic; discernible stress on the final syllable in trisyllabic forms; stress perceived on final long syllables. LAPSyD adds 'These perceptions of stress may be illusory.'
new_statements.domain_note: Domain as reported: the (phonological) word, by syllable count and syllable weight (monomoraic vs long/CV: syllables). Kham is a word-tone language (two pitch patterns x two voice registers, first-hand in Watters 1971: 42-57); the stress remark is about perceived prominence, which LAPSyD judges functionless and possibly illusory. Watters 1971: 57 notes that CVC and CV: syllables are higher in pitch than CV syllables in polysyllabic stems, which may be the phonetic basis of the 'final long syllable' perception.
new_statements.identity_note: All primary sources describe the Takale (Taka-Sera, Baglung/Rukum) dialect of Kham, i.e. Western Parbate Kham west2420 / kjl (Watters 1971: 2 names the dialect and informant; LAPSyD entry is 'Kham, Takale dialect'; WALS kmh maps to west2420). Wilde 2016, also saved, describes Gamale Kham (gama1251 / kgj), a distinct Glottolog language that is atonal, and says nothing about stress.

sources.note: Silent on stress: the words stress/accent/prominence do not occur anywhere in the 57 pp. (segmentals, III The Syllable pp. 35-41, IV Tone pp. 42-57). Tone = two pitch patterns x two voice registers, domain = phonological word; p. 57: 'Any CVC or CV: syllable in a poly-syllabic stem is higher in pitch than an otherwise identical CV syllable'; intonation = pitch drop-off on the last syllable of a sentence. Dialect: Taka (Baglung) / Sera (Rukum), i.e. west2420. (sil.org direct download could not be reached by automated download; identical file taken via the the Internet Archive.)

sources.citation: Watters, David E. (1985). Emergent word tone in Kham: the evolution of a Tibeto-Burman halfway. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 8. pp. 36-54.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Read in full. Nothing on where Kham word stress falls; the 'non-shwa' remark (no vowel reduction on any syllable) is compatible with the catalog's LAPSyD-derived 'no discernable stress' but is not a stress statement. Describes Kham generally (Taka dialect named on p. 49 for the retention of prefixed *r-).

sources.citation: Watters, David E. 1985. Emergent word tone in Kham: a Tibeto-Burman halfway house. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 8(2): 36-54. doi:10.32655/ltba.8.2.02
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No Kham stress rule. Only 'stress' passages are general (SE Asian 'weak or unstressed syllables', Matisoff's schwa mechanism, Mazaudon's remark that in Bodish 'all the syllables have the same stress'); Kham is called a 'non-shwa' language with full vocalic distinctiveness on every syllable (p. 38); 'destressing' of recessive stems mentioned speculatively (p. 51). Confirms the earlier scan note.
